chunks: Prayer is three thirds: a third is purification (tahur), a third is ruku', and a third is sujud. There is no prayer without purification.
Wudu is performed once [for each washing], and whoever performs wudu twice it is permissible, but he receives no reward for it.
All water is pure until it is known to be impure, and nothing corrupts water except that which has a coursing soul (flowing blood).
There is no objection to performing wudu with rosewater and doing ghusl al-janaba with it.

As for water heated by the sun, there is no objection to performing wudu with it, though it is only disliked (makruh) to perform wudu with it, wash clothes with it, or bathe with it, because it causes vitiligo.
Water, when it reaches the quantity of a kurr, nothing makes it najis; the kurr is one thousand two hundred rotl by the Iraqi measure.
And it is also narrated that the kurr is what measures three hand-spans in length, three hand-spans in width, and three hand-spans in depth.
Well water is entirely a purifier (tahur) as long as nothing falls into it making it najis. Seawater is entirely a purifier.

key_terms.الْبَرَص: Baras — vitiligo or leprosy; a skin condition believed in traditional medicine to be caused by washing with sun-heated water
key_terms.الْجَنَابَة: Janaba — major ritual impurity requiring ghusl (full bath), typically from sexual intercourse or seminal emission
key_terms.طَهُور: Tahur — water that is both pure and purifying; the ablution that makes one ritually clean for prayer
key_terms.كُرّ: Kurr — the minimum quantity of water (1200 Iraqi rotl or 3x3x3 hand-spans) that is not rendered najis by contact with impurities
key_terms.نَفْس سَائِلَة: Coursing soul — an animal or creature that has flowing blood; its death in water renders the water najis

ai.seo_question: What are the Islamic rulings on ritual purity (tahara), water, and the kurr measurement according to Shia fiqh?
ai.summary: This text presents a series of jurisprudential rulings (fiqh) on ritual purity (tahara) and prayer, likely transmitted from one of the early Shia Imams. The assembly context is the Ninety-Third Assembly of Sheikh al-Saduq (d. 381 AH), dated 368 AH. It establishes foundational principles: prayer's three essential components, the presumption of water's purity, special rulings on rosewater and sun-heated water, and the kurr standard for water that resists impurity — a crucial measurement in Shia fiqh that remains in use today.
